newsitem.title: UK: British inquiry on foiled N.Irish prison break.
newsitem.headline: British inquiry on foiled N.Irish prison break.

text.p: Britain announced an inquiry on Tuesday into a foiled jail-break by IRA guerrillas at Northern Ireland's maximum security Maze Prison.
Its Northern Ireland Office (NIO) said the investigation, headed by a senior NIO official, would try to uncover how work on a 13-metre (42-foot) tunnel went unnoticed until last Sunday.

The security breach, seen as a major embarrassment in Britain's most heavily guarded prison complex, angered Protestant supporters of rule from London and led to claims that Irish guerrillas have a free rein in their cell blocks.

Security sources say they suspect Irish Republican Army (IRA) fighters had planned a spectacular breakout next weekend to coincide with annual commemorations of their "fight for Irish freedom", or in the leadup to Britain's May 1 election.
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew, who announced the inquiry, told reporters in Belfast that "plainly there are lessons that are to be be learnt".
But it was "quite wrong to say...that the shots are called by the inmates," he said.

A balance must be struck between keeping the prisoners secure and operating a manageable regime, he said. "It may well be that the balance is not correct at the moment, that is why I am establishing this inquiry."
The tunnel, which came within 30 metres (100 feet) of the perimeter wall of the heavily guarded complex, led from a cell in a block housing 95 of the prison's 297 IRA men.
It had been fitted with electric lighting and shored up with makeshift supports. Media reports said it involved the removal of around 13 tonnes of soil. Rubble was found later in searches of cells.
The prison holds around 500 IRA and pro-British Loyalist guerrillas in segregated blocks.
The NIO said its director of policing and security, John Steele, who is a former prisons controller for the province, would supervise the inquiry.
